title: Sweep Line: Minimum Meeting Rooms
oneLiner: The number of rooms you need is the largest number of meetings running at the same moment: sweep through the start and end times in order and track how many are open.
keyTakeaway: Which meeting ends doesn't matter, only WHEN one ends. Sort the start times and the end times separately and walk the starts in order: if the earliest unused end time is <= this start, a room has freed up, so reuse it; otherwise open a new room. The count of rooms ever opened is the answer, in O(n log n).
explanation:
Given meetings as [start, end) pairs, return the minimum number of rooms so that no two meetings in the same room overlap. A meeting that ends at time t frees its room for one that starts at t. For [[0, 30], [5, 10], [15, 20]] the answer is 2: [0, 30] needs its own room the whole time, and the other two can share a second one.

The minimum number of rooms equals the largest number of meetings in progress at any single moment. Fewer rooms can't work at that moment, and that many is always enough, because a room can be handed to the next meeting as soon as it frees up. So the question becomes: what's the peak overlap? Imagine a vertical line sweeping left to right along the time axis. Every start time it crosses adds one meeting in progress, every end time removes one, and you record the highest count. That's the sweep line technique.

You don't need to keep start and end paired up for this, because the sweep only cares about how many meetings are open, not which ones. Sort all the starts and, separately, all the ends. Walk the starts in order with a second pointer e into the ends. For each start s: if ends[e] <= s, some meeting has already finished, so this meeting can take its room (advance e, room count unchanged); otherwise every room is busy, so open a new one. The number of rooms opened is the peak overlap. Sorting dominates: O(n log n) time, O(n) for the two sorted arrays.

The <= is the half-open rule: a meeting ending at 10 and one starting at 10 can share a room. Use < instead and those two would need separate rooms. An equally good alternative uses a min-heap of end times for the rooms in use: sort meetings by start, and for each one, pop the heap's top if it's <= this start (that room is free), then push this meeting's end. The heap's final size is the answer. The same sweep counts peak concurrent users, overlapping flights at an airport, or the busiest moment in a log of sessions.

The visualization sweeps [[0, 30], [5, 10], [10, 20], [25, 35]] as one sorted timeline of events, with ends processed before starts at the same time, which is the same rule as the <= above.

recognitionSignals: "Minimum number of rooms / machines / platforms / servers" so that overlapping intervals never share one.
The answer is a COUNT of the maximum overlap at any moment, not a list of merged ranges.
Events with a start and an end where only how many are active at a time matters, not which ones.
gotchas: Ties decide the answer: with half-open meetings a room freed at t can be reused by a meeting starting at t, so compare with ends[e] <= start (or process ends before starts at the same time).
Sorting the [start, end] pairs by start and only comparing neighbors misses meetings that overlap something further back; you need either the separately sorted ends or a heap of end times.
Merging overlapping intervals and counting the merged blocks gives the number of busy STRETCHES, not the number of rooms; [0, 30], [5, 10], [15, 20] merge into one block but need two rooms.
confusableWith: Merge Intervals (this track) combines overlapping intervals into blocks; here overlapping intervals are exactly the ones that must stay APART, and the answer is the peak overlap count.

Top-K with a Heap (this track): a min-heap of end times for the rooms in use is a valid alternative solution (pop when the earliest end is <= the next start); the sweep over two sorted arrays gets the same count without a heap.

complexity.note: Sorting the start times and end times dominates; the two-pointer sweep after it is O(n). The heap-of-end-times version has the same bounds.

referenceSolutions.python:
def min_meeting_rooms(intervals):
    starts = sorted(iv[0] for iv in intervals)
    ends = sorted(iv[1] for iv in intervals)
    rooms = 0
    e = 0
    for s in starts:
        if s >= ends[e]:  # the earliest-ending meeting is over: reuse its room
            e += 1
        else:
            rooms += 1  # every room is busy: open a new one
    return rooms
